I can see how the sidenotes are supposed to work. The implementation is based on the Tufte CSS design principles, where sidenotes appear in the margin on desktop and inline on mobile. Here's how it should work:

1. **Desktop View (> 760px)**:
   - Sidenotes float to the right margin
   - They take up 50% width and are positioned with a -60% right margin
   - Clicking the number highlights the corresponding note
   - Notes are styled in a lighter color (var(--side-note-color))

2. **Mobile View (≤ 760px)**:
   - Sidenotes display inline as blocks
   - They have a left border in the accent color
   - They take up 95% width
   - Clicking the number scrolls to the note and highlights it

3. **Interactive Features**:
   - Numbers are clickable (in red/accent color)
   - Clicking toggles highlighting of the note
   - On mobile, clicking also scrolls to the note
   - There's a global state system to track which note is currently highlighted

We need to create a React version of the MarginNote component that uses the same global highlight state system. Let me create that first:

```diff

+ import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
+ 
+ // Import the same global state management from SidenoteReact
+ const subscribers = new Set<(id: string | null) => void>();
+ let currentHighlightedId: string | null = null;
+ 
+ const subscribeToHighlight = (callback: (id: string | null) => void): () => void => {
+   subscribers.add(callback);
+   return () => {
+     subscribers.delete(callback);
+   };
+ };
+ 
+ const setHighlightedNote = (id: string | null): void => {
+   currentHighlightedId = id;
+   subscribers.forEach(callback => callback(id));
+ };
+ 
+ interface MarginNoteProps {
+   children: React.ReactNode;
+   id?: string;
+ }
+ 
+ export default function MarginNoteReact({ children, id = `mn-${Math.random().toString(36).substr(2, 9)}` }: MarginNoteProps) {
+   const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = useState(false);
+   const [isHighlighted, setIsHighlighted] = useState(false);
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     const checkMobile = () => {
+       setIsMobile(window.innerWidth < 760);
+     };
+     
+     checkMobile();
+     window.addEventListener('resize', checkMobile);
+     return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', checkMobile);
+   }, []);
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     const unsubscribe = subscribeToHighlight((highlightedId) => {
+       setIsHighlighted(highlightedId === id);
+     });
+     return unsubscribe;
+   }, [id]);
+ 
+   const handleClick = () => {
+     if (isHighlighted) {
+       setHighlightedNote(null);
+     } else {
+       setHighlightedNote(id);
+       if (isMobile) {
+         const element = document.getElementById(id);
+         element?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' });
+       }
+     }
+   };
+ 
+   return (
+     <span
+       id={id}
+       onClick={handleClick}
+       className={`margin-note ${isHighlighted ? 'highlighted' : ''} ${isMobile ? 'mobile' : ''}`}
+       style={{ cursor: 'pointer' }}
+     >
+       {children}
+     </span>
+   );
+ } 
```

In your browser, you can check mobile view in a few ways:

1. **Using Browser Dev Tools (Easiest)**:
   - Press `F12` or right-click and select "Inspect"
   - Click the "Toggle device toolbar" button (looks like a phone/tablet icon) or press `Ctrl+Shift+M`
   - You can then select different device presets or manually set the width below 760px (our mobile breakpoint)

2. **Manual Window Resizing**:
   - Simply drag your browser window to make it narrower than 760px

3. **Device Emulation**:
   - In Chrome Dev Tools, you can select specific device models (like iPhone or Pixel) from a dropdown in the device toolbar

The sidenotes and margin notes will switch to mobile view when the viewport width is less than 760px. In mobile view, you'll see:
- Notes appear inline instead of in the margin
- Notes have a left border in the accent color
- Clicking a note will scroll it into view
- Only one note can be highlighted at a time

Try resizing your browser window or using the device toolbar to test the responsive behavior!

_**Assistant**_



Let me explain running a production build locally in simple terms:

When you're developing your website, you're running it in "development mode" - it's like having training wheels on a bike. This mode includes extra checks and warnings to help you catch mistakes, but it makes the site run a bit slower.

To run a production build locally:

1. Open your terminal
2. Make sure you're in your project folder
3. Type this command:
```bash
npm run build
```

This will:
- Create a special version of your website that's optimized for real users
- Remove all the development-only warnings and checks
- Package everything up like it would be on Vercel

Then to test this production version locally, you can run:
```bash
npm run preview
```

This lets you see exactly how your site will behave when it's live on Vercel, without those development warnings we're seeing now.

if I do this, can I delete it later when I change things?

_**Assistant**_



Yes, absolutely! The build process creates a temporary production version that you can safely delete or overwrite. Here's how it works:

1. When you run `npm run build`:
   - It creates a `dist` folder (or similar, depending on your setup)
   - This folder contains the production version
   - It's completely separate from your source code

2. You can:
   - Delete the `dist` folder anytime
   - Run `npm run build` again when you make changes
   - Your original code in `src` stays untouched

It's like making a photocopy of your document:
- Your original document (source code) stays safe
- You can make as many copies (builds) as you want
- Throw away the copies whenever you want
- Make new copies when you need them

Would you like to try it out? You can always delete the build folder right after testing!

_**Assistant**_



Let me understand this:
1. `npm run build` + `npm run preview` - theme toggle works
2. Opening the `index.html` file directly - theme toggle doesn't work

This is normal! The difference is because:

1. When you open `index.html` directly in a browser:
   - It uses the `file://` protocol
   - Local storage doesn't work properly
   - Some browser security features block it

2. When you use `npm run preview`:
   - It runs a proper web server
   - Uses the `http://` protocol
   - Everything works as expected

This is why we always need to use a server (like `npm run preview` or `npm run dev`) to test the site, rather than opening the HTML files directly. When you deploy to Vercel, it will work fine because:
1. Vercel provides a proper web server
2. The site will be served over `https://`
3. All browser features (like localStorage) will work correctly

So no need to worry - if it works with `npm run preview`, it will work on Vercel too!

```jsx
import Sidenote from '../components/Sidenote.astro';

Here's some text<Sidenote number={1}>With a sidenote</Sidenote>
```

- Everything now lives in root, making it simpler

Here's how the interactive parts work in the main site:

1. **Sidenotes**
```markdown
# How to use in content:
Here's text<Sidenote number={1}>This is a sidenote</Sidenote>
Or a margin note<MarginNote>This appears in margin</MarginNote>
```

2. **How Sidenotes Work**
- Desktop: Notes float in right margin
- Mobile: Notes move to end of paragraphs
- Click numbers to highlight notes
- Mobile has a toggle button (circle with "1") to show/hide all notes
- State managed by simple pub/sub in `noteState.ts`

3. **Dark Mode**
- Toggle in bottom right corner
- Saves preference in localStorage
- Uses CSS variables for colors:
```css
:root {
  --background-color: #faf8f1;  /* light mode */
  --text-color: #222;
  --accent-color: #a00000;
  /* etc */
}

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --background-color: #1a1a1a;  /* dark mode */
  /* etc */
}
```

4. **Layout**
- Everything wrapped in `Layout.astro`
- Handles the nav header
- Includes theme and sidenote toggles
- Responsive design (breaks at 760px)

That's the main functionality - sidenotes that work differently on mobile/desktop, and a persistent dark mode. Everything else is just standard Astro/MDX content.
